:::{#def-loss-function}
#### Loss function

A **loss function** $L(y, \hy)$ is a rule that gives a number that is 0 or larger:
the cost of [predicting](#def-prediction) $\hy$ when the true value is $y$
[@wikipedia_loss_function].

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-loss-function}
#### A loss function that charges more for overpredicting

Let $L(y, \hy)$ cost $2$ per unit of overprediction and $1$ per unit of underprediction:

$$
L(y, \hy) =
\begin{cases}
2\paren{\hy - y} & \text{if } \hy > y \\
y - \hy & \text{if } \hy \le y.
\end{cases}
$$

This is a [loss function](#def-loss-function) because it is never negative.
For the true value $y = 2$ and the prediction $\hy = 7$,
the loss is $L(2, 7) = 2 \cd 5 = 10$.
For $y = 7$ and $\hy = 2$, the loss is $L(7, 2) = 5$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-squared-error-loss}
#### Squared error loss

The **squared error loss** is the [loss function](#def-loss-function)
that charges the square of the difference between the true value $y$ and the [prediction](#def-prediction) $\hy$:

$$L(y, \hy) \eqdef \sqf{y - \hy}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-squared-error-loss}
#### Squared error loss for one prediction

For the true value $y = 2$ and the prediction $\hy = 7$,
the [squared error loss](#def-squared-error-loss) is

$$\sqf{2 - 7} = 25.$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-absolute-error-loss}
#### Absolute error loss

The **absolute error loss** is the [loss function](#def-loss-function)
that charges the absolute value of the difference between the true value $y$ and the [prediction](#def-prediction) $\hy$:

$$L(y, \hy) \eqdef \abs{y - \hy}$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-absolute-error-loss}
#### Absolute error loss for one prediction

For the true value $y = 2$ and the prediction $\hy = 7$,
the [absolute error loss](#def-absolute-error-loss) is

$$\abs{2 - 7} = 5.$$

:::

::: {#rem-squared-error-loss-common}
#### Squared error loss is the most common choice

@hastie2009elements [p. 18] call squared error loss
"by far the most common and convenient" choice.

:::
